Program:
double price = 3.14159;
System.out.printf("%6.2f", price);
System.out.printf("|%d items%n", 4);

Question: What is printed, exactly (count the spaces)? Explain each format specifier.

Student's answer: "With %.3f it would print 3.142 and no spaces. price itself is still 3.14159; only the printed digits change."

Concept under consideration: formatted_output

Candidate edges of this concept. A misconception/error edge shows the wrong rule (logic) and the right rule (twin_logic); a concept edge shows the rule that links the two concepts; a level way (lvl:) shows one way an answer can display a level of understanding of the concept.
- lvl:formatted_output@L0#0 | level L0 way everyday_reading: In maths `7.2` (or %2.4f) reads as a decimal number, or as '7 digits before the point, 2 after'. In a format specifier the number before the point is the total field width and the number after it is the digits after the decimal point. Also `%` is not 'percent'.
- lvl:formatted_output@L0#4 | level L0 way inconsistent_trace: Points to LT (specifiers are paired with arguments left to right, and the other characters pass through). An uneven trace pairs a specifier with the wrong argument, drops the literal text between specifiers, or pads on the wrong side on some fields. (here mixing in: "Any conversion code (%d, %f, %s) works with any argument type")
- lvl:formatted_output@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: printf is the formatted-print method of standard output. It takes a format string and arguments and writes the formatted string.
- lvl:formatted_output@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: A format specifier has the form %[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion: d for integer types, f for floating-point values, s for String or any type. The width is a minimum character count, and for f the precision is the number of digits after the point.
- lvl:formatted_output@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: The arguments are evaluated first. The format string is then scanned left to right: ordinary characters are copied, and each specifier takes the next argument, converts it, rounds it to the precision and pads it with blanks to the width (left side by default, right side with the `-` flag).
- lvl:formatted_output@L2#1 | level L2 way output_prediction: The output is the formatted text. printf("%7.5f", Math.PI) gives 3.14159, printf("PI is approximately %.2f\n", Math.PI) gives `PI is approximately 3.14` and a newline, and printf("%5d", 42) gives `   42`. Rounding is half-up.
- lvl:formatted_output@L2#2 | level L2 way one_step_execution: One call appends one formatted string to standard output and adds no newline unless \n or %n is in the format. The stored values of the arguments do not change (only their printed form is rounded).
- lvl:formatted_output@L3#0 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: printf output goes into the same stream as print/println and lands at the point in the stream where it was called. It does not end the line.
- lvl:formatted_output@L3#1 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: println prints a double with all its digits (about 15 places) and always ends the line. printf("%.2f\n", x) controls the digits and ends the line only because of \n.
- lvl:formatted_output@L3#2 | level L3 way purpose_of_the_whole: Plan: table printing. Inside a loop, one fixed format string with a specifier per column prints aligned rows (e.g. a loan table) at a chosen precision.
- lvl:formatted_output@L4#0 | level L4 way predict_a_change: Changing the precision changes only the printed digits, not the stored value. Changing the width changes only the padding. A width smaller than the converted text is ignored, so nothing is truncated.
- lvl:formatted_output@L4#1 | level L4 way transfer_to_a_new_program: Use printf when the number of digits, the field width or column alignment matters (tables, money, reports). For quick checks of a value, println is enough.
- lvl:formatted_output@L4#2 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: The conversion code must match the argument type. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: %d with a double, or %f with an int (e.g. printf("%4.2f", 512)): IllegalFormatConversionException.
- lvl:formatted_output@L4#3 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: There must be an argument for every specifier, and the format syntax must be legal. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: More specifiers than arguments (e.g. printf("%d %d", 3)), or a malformed specifier: an IllegalFormatException subclass such as MissingFormatArgumentException.
- lvl:formatted_output@L4#4 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: printf adds no line separator. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A printf in a loop without \n: all rows run together on one line.
